---
title: "Week 11 — AI use and judgments of competence"
description: "How evaluators judge AI-assisted work, and whether status changes those judgments"
---

## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">When is using AI perceived as resourceful, and when is it perceived as lazy or incompetent? Does the worker’s status affect that judgment?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 10 considered how people interpret AI-assisted messages between friends and colleagues. This week moves to evaluation at work. An employee’s report may be accurate and useful, yet readers may judge the writer differently when told that AI helped produce it. We ask whether such judgments also depend on who the writer is.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of class, you should be able to:

- explain the AI-use evaluation penalty identified by Reif and colleagues, without treating it as evidence of a class difference;
- describe Foschi’s account of status-based standards for competence;
- explain how Rafalow’s schools assigned different value to similar digital practices;
- distinguish competence, laziness, trust and the perceived legitimacy of AI assistance;
- use a nested Python loop to prepare four versions of one report for a proposed human-reader experiment.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Status and competence:** Martha Foschi (2000), “Double Standards for Competence: Theory and Research,” *Annual Review of Sociology* 26: 21–42. A review of research on how status can change the evidence observers require before judging someone competent. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.soc.26.1.21). [@Foschi2000DoubleStandards]
- **Judging AI users:** Jessica A. Reif, Richard P. Larrick and Jack B. Soll (2025), “Evidence of a Social Evaluation Penalty for Using Artificial Intelligence,” *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* 122: e2426766122. Experiments in which observers rate workers who use AI, receive human help or work without described help. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2426766122). [@ReifLarrickSoll2025]
- **Digital skill in schools:** Matthew H. Rafalow (2018), “Disciplining Play: Digital Youth Culture as Capital at School,” *American Journal of Sociology* 123(5): 1416–1452. Ethnographic evidence that teachers in three schools attached different educational value to students’ digital practices. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1086/695766). [@Rafalow2018DiscipliningPlay]
- **Disclosure and trust:** Oliver Schilke and Martin Reimann (2025), “The Transparency Dilemma: How AI Disclosure Erodes Trust,” *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes* 188: 104405. Experiments on trust in people who disclose AI assistance; Study 11 concerns a monthly competitor report. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104405). [@SchilkeReimann2025Transparency]
:::

## Sociological and methodological background

Foschi reviews studies in which observers apply different standards of competence to people with different social statuses. A performance does not necessarily carry the same evidentiary weight when the performer changes. This is a reason to test how a senior executive and a junior employee are judged for the same AI-assisted report, not a prediction whose direction we already know. A senior professional might receive more credit for using a tool efficiently; that professional might instead be penalized more for failing to exercise expected independent expertise. Foschi discusses both ordinary and reverse double standards. [@Foschi2000DoubleStandards]

Bourdieu’s linguistic market asks how speech and writing acquire value in a particular setting and why speakers do not enter that setting with equal authority. Lamont and Lareau press us to identify which signals an institution actually recognizes as valuable. These arguments suggest that a polished report alone will not tell us what readers infer about its author. They do not establish an AI-specific penalty. [@Bourdieu1977Linguistic; @LamontLareau1988CulturalCapital]

Rafalow observed three schools in which teachers responded differently to students’ digital creativity: as irrelevant, threatening or useful for learning. The schools differed in race, class and institutional context together. His study does not isolate a class effect or examine ChatGPT. It does show why we should study the evaluator and setting rather than assume that a digital practice has the same meaning wherever it appears. [@Rafalow2018DiscipliningPlay]

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Reif, Larrick and Soll ran four preregistered experiments on how people judge AI users. In Study 2, workers described as using AI were rated lazier than workers receiving comparable human help or no described help; they were also rated lower on competence and related traits. The study did not find significant moderation by age, gender or occupation. It therefore gives us evidence of an AI-use evaluation penalty, but not of the specific senior–junior interaction proposed for this class. [@ReifLarrickSoll2025]

Schilke and Reimann study trust in people who disclose AI assistance. In their Study 11, participants judged a market research analyst’s monthly competitor report. The design varied both prior knowledge of AI use and disclosure with the report. Mean trust was 4.10 with disclosure and 4.62 without it; the no-disclosure condition did not affirmatively claim that no AI was used. Their wider series examines whether the assistance is considered a legitimate way to complete the task. This is not a test of different occupational ranks. Trust and competence should be measured separately in a new study. [@SchilkeReimann2025Transparency]

Our proposed experiment keeps a fictional competitor report identical while changing two descriptions: whether the author is a senior executive or junior employee, and whether AI use is disclosed. Human readers could rate competence, laziness, trust and the acceptability of AI assistance. The Python exercise prepares these four materials; it does not collect ratings. Occupational rank is a status cue, not a direct measure of social class. A real study would need to pretest what readers infer from the roles and consider whether different job duties change what they expect.

## Reading discussion

1. What exactly do Reif’s participants evaluate? How is that different from judging the quality of the work itself?
2. Foschi allows more than one prediction about a senior and a junior worker. Which expectations would produce each result?
3. What does Rafalow show about who gets to define digital skill as valuable? Which parts of his comparison cannot be attributed to class alone?
4. Why might the AI disclosure in Schilke and Reimann’s competitor-report study lower trust? Would that necessarily imply lower perceived competence?
5. What would we need to observe before concluding that the AI penalty differs by class rather than by job rank or task expectations?

## Take-home exercise

Use the fictional report to request one careful model edit. Check the raw response against the stated facts, including the absence of customer-switching data. Then use a nested loop to place the same revised report in four hypothetical descriptions varying the author’s role and reported AI use. Trace the first two passes and explain what human judgments a real experiment would still need.

Follow the [recording and submission instructions](../recording-and-submission.qmd), name the file with your name and `Week11`, and submit by **5:00 p.m. Eastern on the Tuesday before the next class**.

## Summary and preparation

The existing experiments document penalties in how AI users are judged. Foschi, Bourdieu, Lamont and Lareau, and Rafalow help us ask whether those judgments depend on social position and institutional standards. We do not yet have evidence that the penalty is larger for a junior employee. The proposed four-condition study would test that question against the possibility of a larger penalty for the senior employee.
